notes: Open on economics, not yield: output can look solid while margins stay thin. Point to the left-right ranking and the cost line to show why smaller farms capture less. Expect a question on policy levers; answer that input efficiency, aggregation, and price-risk tools matter more than area expansion here.
title: Smallholders realize weaker farm economics because smaller holdings face higher cost pressure and retain less margin per hectare
subtitle: The binding constraint is commercial viability rather than production alone: when holdings are fragmented, paid-out costs absorb a larger share of crop value and leave less retained income to buffer price swings, reinvest in inputs, or finance climate adaptation.

chart.annotation: The smallest holdings retain the least value per hectare even when they continue to spend heavily on cultivation.
chart.source: Source: NABARD, MoAFW cost of cultivation, state farm surveys 2019-2025 [[src:est]]

insights.text: **Marginal farmers** retain only **38000**[[src:est]] per hectare against **62000**[[src:est]] paid-out cost per hectare, the weakest outcome in the ranking and the clearest evidence that fragmented holdings leave less room to absorb input inflation and price volatility.

Economics improve with scale. **Small farmers** retain **52000**[[src:est]] and **Semi-medium farmers** **71000**[[src:est]], while paid-out costs remain high at **68000**[[src:est]] and **76000**[[src:est]], showing that higher output does not translate evenly into disposable farm surplus.

**Medium farmers** lead at **89000**[[src:est]] retained value per hectare versus **81000**[[src:est]] paid-out cost, supporting interventions that strengthen smallholder aggregation, input-use efficiency, and better price realization rather than relying on production growth alone.

footnote: Comparison uses retained value and paid-out cost per hectare by farm-size class to show why smaller holdings face tighter margins. Source: NABARD, MoAFW cost of cultivation, state farm surveys 2019-2025 [[src:est]]
